opus-5.5.text:
I think they'd be pretty inadequate, honestly, at least as the main mechanism we rely on.

Leaks are better than nothing. If something dramatic is happening inside a lab, like AI systems doing most of the research work, or a sudden jump in capability on internal benchmarks, it's quite likely some of that gets out through people talking to friends, journalists, or posting vague things online. But a few things make me skeptical that this would actually trigger a good policy response.

First, the signal is really noisy. There's already a constant stream of hype and vague insider claims, like "you won't believe what we're seeing internally." Policymakers and the public have learned to discount that, and reasonably so, because a lot of it is marketing or excitement. So when the real thing happens, it may sound exactly like everything that came before.

Second, leaks are partial and unverifiable. A policymaker hearing a secondhand rumor that some lab's models are now automating most of their ML research can't act on it the way they could on a rigorous, documented report. They don't know the denominator, how much of the work, compared to what baseline, measured how. Without that, the natural response is to wait and see, and in an intelligence explosion, waiting a few months could matter a lot.

Third, timing. Informal information tends to come out with a lag, and in fragments. If things are moving fast, by the time the picture is clear enough to be compelling, a lot may already be locked in.

And fourth, the incentives cut against it. Staff have NDAs, equity, loyalty to their colleagues, and a real belief that their company is the responsible one. The people with the most detailed knowledge are often the least likely to leak, and the ones who do can be dismissed as disgruntled.

So what I'd want instead is something more structured: regular, mandatory reporting to some part of government on things like internal capability evaluations, how much AI is being used to accelerate AI development itself, and compute usage. Ideally with some verification, and with whistleblower protections as a backstop rather than the primary channel. The point is to have the government already looking at the right indicators, with a baseline, so that when the curve bends, it's legible and it's legible early. Leaks are the thing you fall back on when that system fails, not the system itself.

r001.rationale: The response says informal leaks are noisy, partial, and unverifiable, so policymakers may wait rather than act; it contrasts them with rigorous documented reports and structured government reporting with verification, which are more actionable.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm pretty pessimistic about leaks as the main mechanism. I think they'd be better than nothing, but they're a really thin reed to hang a policy response on, for a few reasons.

The first is just that leaks are noisy and hard to interpret from the outside. Imagine someone at a lab tells a journalist, "Our internal models are now doing most of the work on our next training run." What does a policymaker do with that? They don't know how to weigh it against the company's public statements, which will probably be reassuring. They don't know if this person is disgruntled, or exaggerating, or has an idiosyncratic view of what counts as "most of the work." And in a world where there are already a lot of breathless claims about AI progress floating around, one more anonymous quote doesn't necessarily move anyone.

The second problem is that the people who are best positioned to know what's happening are also the people with the strongest incentives not to talk. If you're on the team that's seeing the first real signs of recursive self-improvement, you're probably under heavy confidentiality obligations, you may have a lot of equity, and you probably believe, at least partly, that your company is the responsible one and it's better that you're ahead. So the information that leaks is going to be selected in strange ways. You might get leaks about culture problems or safety team departures, which are real signals but indirect ones, and not the hard capability numbers that would actually let someone outside assess what's going on.

And then the third thing is timing. If an intelligence explosion is happening on something like months rather than years, the lag between "an employee notices something alarming," "that employee decides to say something," "a reporter verifies it," "it gets enough traction that a congressional staffer reads it," and "there's an actual policy response" is just too long. Our policy institutions move slowly even when the facts are clear, and here the facts would be contested at every step.

So what I'd want instead is something more structured. Mandatory reporting of certain kinds of internal results, things like what fraction of AI R&D is being done autonomously, or capability evaluations on agreed-upon benchmarks, to a government body that has the technical staff to actually interpret them. Whistleblower protections that are specific to AI, so that people who do want to speak up aren't just gambling their careers and legal exposure on it. And ideally some kind of ongoing third-party access, so you're not relying on the lab to tell you what to look at.

I'd also say that I think leaks matter more as a backstop than as a primary mechanism. If you have formal reporting requirements, then the threat of leaks keeps the formal reports honest, because the government can cross-check. Without the formal channel, leaks are the only thing you have, and I think they'd arrive too late and be too ambiguous to do the job. So I'd put it as, leaks are a necessary ingredient in a healthy system but nowhere close to sufficient on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says leaks are noisy, ambiguous, and may not move policymakers, and proposes structured reporting as an alternative. It does not clearly state that salient official information that is not credibly disputed would mobilize policy more effectively.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t want to rely on that. There’s a difference between information getting out and information reaching policymakers in a form that they can understand, verify, and act on. You could have employees saying, “Something really big is happening internally,” and still have a lot of uncertainty about what that means or whether it’s credible.

And if the process is moving quickly, that uncertainty is costly. You don’t want the first step to be figuring out who to believe, the second step to be understanding the implications, and only then starting to work out what the government can actually do.

So I think leaks could help draw attention to something, but they’re a pretty fragile foundation for a policy response. I’d much rather have established channels for reporting concerning developments, people in government with the expertise to assess them, and some advance thinking about what would trigger action. The information is much more useful if there’s already a mechanism for responding to it.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls leaks a fragile foundation for policy action and contrasts them with established reporting channels, government expertise, and predefined triggers, explaining that leaks may be uncertain or hard to verify.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t feel very comfortable relying on that. I think leaks could be useful for getting people’s attention, but there’s a pretty big gap between someone saying, “Something really concerning is happening inside this company,” and policymakers having enough credible, specific information to take action.

The people who know the most might also be uncertain about what they’re seeing. They might disagree with one another, or be reluctant to disclose information that they think is dangerous to make public. And from the government’s perspective, it could be hard to distinguish a serious warning from something exaggerated, especially when there are lots of dramatic claims about AI already.

If things are moving very quickly, you don’t want the first step to be figuring out who to believe and what authority anyone has to intervene. I’d much rather have established channels for reporting concerning capabilities, protections for people who raise alarms, and a government that has enough technical understanding to interpret those reports. Leaks could be a backstop, but I wouldn’t want them to be the main plan.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts leaks that may draw attention but lack credible, specific information for policymakers with established reporting channels that would give government more actionable information.
